newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila says ready to be transit point for defector.
newsitem.headline: Manila says ready to be transit point for defector.

text.p: The Philippines said on Saturday it had been asked to serve as a transit point for a North Korean defector in Beijing if he was allowed to go to South Korea, and it was prepared to agree to the request.

Foreign Secretary Domingo Siazon said the request for the Philippines to accept Hwang Jang-yop, a North Korean ideologue and top aide to supreme leader Kim Jong-il, in transit was made by South Korea and China.

"There are talks going on based on the request of the Republic of Korea and also China to find a way of having this gentleman go to his destination without going through a straight route, and we have been asked," Siazon said.

"Our view is if the three countries concerned are informed and we are being asked to find a solution, then in order to make our contribution to resolving this problem -- because we are all in Asia -- we don't wish this particular problem to evolve into a more serious politicial difficulty among the three parties, so we would in that context be prepared to make our contribution."

Siazon, speaking to reporters before he left for an official visit to Japan, stressed it was not "categorically sure" the Philippines would be a transit point for any transfer of Hwang, adding other routes might be under study.
"Whether that gentleman will pass here or not we do not really know. Maybe there are some other routes being considered," he said.
He said he thought the Philippines was considered a possible stop-off point because "we are a neutral country."
"I suppose only for a short duration," he said when asked how long Hwang would stay on Philippine soil if he was allowed to go to South Korea and the Philippines was chosen as transit point.
"What is important here apparently is the symbolic notion that he touched ground here or he touched another country's ground before proceeding so that the routing is not directly done," Siazon added.
He said if the transit was made in the Philippines, it would not be carried out by the Department of Foreign Affairs but by "the military people." He did not elaborate.

Asked if Hwang might transit through Subic Bay, a former U.S. naval facility north of Manila and now a freeport with an international airport of its own, Siazon said: "I don't really know. The Philippines is composed of 7,107 islands. I'm not involved in the details of any plans of this nature."

Hwang has been stranded at the South Korean consular compound in Beijing since February 12. He is the most senior official to defect from North Korea and talks have been taking place between the two Koreas and China on his fate.
Chinese premier Li Peng said on Friday that China wanted a swift end to the crisis.
Hwang has said he wants to go to South Korea and foreign diplomats said that he would likely be allowed to leave for a third country first and then travel to Seoul.
